title: Watching him walk
hookLine: the old brahmin's pupil follows the Buddha for months, watching how he walks and eats

lines: WATCH THEM ON AN ORDINARY DAY.
cards: How do you really get to know someone? Not their profile, not their speeches. You watch them on an ordinary day: how they treat a waiter, how they eat when they think nobody's looking.

In the city of Mithilā lives a well-known brahmin named Brahmāyu, a master of the old Vedic learning, and the sutta says he's a hundred and twenty years old. He hears the Buddha is nearby, and he does something careful.
He sends his best student, a young man named Uttara, to watch. Not to debate. To watch.

teach.b: Uttara follows the Buddha for seven months, the sutta says, like a shadow that never leaves. Then he goes home and reports, down to the smallest movement. When he walks, he steps off with the right foot.

teach.h: RIGHT FOOT FIRST, NEITHER FAST NOR SLOW.
teach.b: His stride is neither too long nor too short, neither too fast nor too slow. His knees and ankles don't knock together. When he looks back, he turns his whole body, the way an elephant does.

When he sits down in a house, he doesn't drop into the seat or fidget once he's there. When he eats, he takes rice and curry in proportion, and turns each mouthful over two or three times before swallowing.
He tastes the food, the report says, but without greed for the taste. After eating he sits in silence for a while, then gives a blessing for the meal, and he doesn't find fault with the food.
When he teaches, his voice is clear and carries exactly as far as the gathering, and no farther. And so it goes: robes, bowl, washing, sleeping. Notice what convinces Uttara.
Not an argument. Not a wonder.

teach.h: THE SAME IN THE KITCHEN AS ON THE SEAT.
teach.b: A man who is the same in the kitchen as on the teaching seat.
Brahmāyu hears the report, bows in the Buddha's direction, and later goes to meet him. The sutta says he understood the teaching that day and died not long after.
A hundred and twenty years old, and what first reached him was a description of someone eating rice.

how: Monastic training in Buddhist traditions gives careful attention to deportment, how to walk, sit, eat and wear robes, and lay Buddhists often say they learned most from watching how a respected teacher lives day to day.

o: deportment: how you walk, stand, sit and lie down
the road a monk follows on his daily alms round
a walking path laid out around a temple or stupa

p: right foot first, neither fast nor slow
turns his whole body, like an elephant
his voice carries just to the gathering

s: Brahmāyu sent Uttara to debate the Buddha
he sent him to watch, and Uttara followed him for seven months.
the report says the Buddha turned each mouthful over two or three times
and tasted the food without greed for the taste.
Uttara was convinced by a miracle
he was convinced by ordinary conduct: walking, sitting, eating, teaching.

games.q: you're Brahmāyu, a hundred and twenty years old. you want to know if a well-known teacher is the real thing. what do you do?
o: send your best student to argue with him
send your best student to watch him live
games.why: Brahmāyu sends Uttara to watch. seven months of ordinary days tell him more than any debate.

practice: Picture someone whose goodness you trust, not for what they say but for how they are, doing something ordinary: walking into a room, eating, answering a phone. Notice what you see.
Then, for the rest of the sit, turn the same quiet attention on yourself: how you're sitting, how you're breathing, right now.

wordCard.voice: Iriyapatha. Uttara followed the Buddha for seven months and reported how he walked, sat and ate. What convinced him was the ordinary.

orig.note: Pali iriyāpatha: deportment, the postures of walking, standing, sitting and lying down.

carryVoice: Your line: watch how they walk. Goodness shows in the kitchen as much as on the teaching seat. Day four hundred seventy-four, done.
